questions.q: What was the immediate constitutional trigger for the 1971 crisis in Pakistan, and which party won the 1970 general elections with a clear majority in the National Assembly?
questions.a: The immediate trigger was President Yahya Khan's postponement of the National Assembly session (scheduled for 3 March 1971) after the Awami League, led by Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, won 160 of 162 East Pakistan seats and an absolute majority (167/313) in the National Assembly. The Awami League's Six-Point Programme demanded provincial autonomy. A wrong answer (e.g., "Bhutto's PPP won" or "the crisis started with Indian invasion") reveals confusion about the democratic mandate that West Pakistan refused to honour — the core political cause of the war.

questions.q: Why did India sign the Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation in August 1971, months before the war? Explain the strategic logic.
questions.a: India signed the treaty to deter Chinese and US intervention on Pakistan's side. The US-China-Pakistan axis (evident in Kissinger's secret July 1971 Beijing visit) threatened a two-front war. The treaty's Article 9 mandated mutual consultation if either faced a threat, signalling Soviet backing. A wrong answer (e.g., "India wanted Soviet arms" or "it was ideological") misses the realpolitik: India needed a nuclear umbrella against great-power interference to execute a limited, time-bound military operation — a classic case of alliance-building for deterrence (linking to c12_ps_cbse_05_002's balance-of-power concept).

questions.q: A student argues: "India intervened in East Pakistan only because of the refugee burden; without 10 million refugees, India would have stayed out." Evaluate this claim using evidence from India's diplomatic record (April–November 1971).
questions.a: The claim is partially true but incomplete. The refugee crisis (10 million by November 1971, costing ₹7 crore daily) made the status quo unsustainable, but India's strategy was calibrated: (1) PM Indira Gandhi's global tour (Oct–Nov 1971) sought political recognition of Bangladesh's cause, not just refugee relief; (2) India trained Mukti Bahini from April 1971, before the refugee peak; (3) the Indo-Soviet Treaty (August) was a strategic pre-commitment. A wrong answer ignoring the diplomatic-military preparation reveals a humanitarian-only lens, missing the realist calculation that a hostile East Pakistan was a permanent strategic threat.

questions.q: Compare the 1971 war's outcome with the 1965 India-Pakistan war (covered in c12_ps_cbse_05_002) in terms of: (a) territorial changes, (b) strategic doctrine, (c) great-power involvement.
questions.a: (a) 1965: No territorial change (Tashkent restored status quo); 1971: Pakistan lost 56% population, 23% territory, and 93,000 PoWs — a permanent geopolitical shift. (b) 1965: Limited war aiming at Kashmir; 1971: Decisive war aiming at liberation, using Blitzkrieg-style combined arms. (c) 1965: US/UK arms embargo hurt both; 1971: US tilted to Pakistan (Task Force 74), USSR backed India (vetoed UN ceasefire). A wrong answer treating both as "stalemates" misses 1971's transformative character — it ended the two-nation theory's territorial expression and established India's regional primacy.

questions.q: The Shimla Agreement (1972) is often called "India's magnanimity." Critique this view by analyzing its three core provisions and their long-term enforcement.
questions.a: The Agreement: (1) Bilateralism — all disputes to be settled peacefully without third parties; (2) LoC in J&K recognized as "ceasefire line" to be respected; (3) 93,000 PoWs returned unconditionally. "Magnanimity" is a misreading: India traded PoWs for bilateralism (denying Pakistan UN/internationalization of Kashmir) and LoC sanctity. However, Pakistan violated bilateralism by raising Kashmir at UN/OIC, and the LoC became militarized (Siachen 1984, Kargil 1999). A wrong answer calling it "generous" ignores that India extracted maximum strategic concessions (bilateral framework, LoC legitimacy) while releasing PoWs it couldn't indefinitely hold — a realist bargain, not altruism.

questions.q: Draft a 150-word policy memo for a 1972 Indian Foreign Service officer explaining why the 1971 victory did NOT guarantee enduring regional stability, identifying three structural fault lines that would resurface.
questions.a: A strong memo identifies: (1) **Pakistan's revisionism** — the military-jihadi complex would reinterpret 1971 as betrayal, not defeat, fueling proxy war (Khalistan, Kashmir insurgency); (2) **Unresolved border/river disputes** — 6.1 km undemarcated land boundary, Teesta/Feni water sharing, enclaves (resolved only in 2015); (3) **Bangladesh's domestic volatility** — Mujib's assassination (1975), military coups, and Islamist resurgence would complicate India's "friendly neighbour" assumption. A weak memo lists only "Pakistan hatred" or "economic problems," missing the structural-institutional drivers: Pakistan's identity crisis, India's federal water disputes, and Bangladesh's fragile democratic consolidation.
